HN candidate 'Show HN: Sphinx - A hook that quizzes you on your AI's code before shipping' with 253 points and 89 comments (2026-10-18, item 50137950, author critiquebrowser). Sphinx is a Git hook for agent-assisted development, published on npm as sphinx-understand (version 0.1.13, MIT). It sets the global Git core.hooksPath and chains pre-existing hooks, then a push to a protected branch waits while a reviewer model reads the committed change through read-only Git tools and asks the developer a question. The reviewer runs in a separate context from the coding agent and never sees the conversation that produced the code, so it grades the diff rather than the prompt. Questions cover behavior, failure modes and invariants rather than file names, and the check is open book: the developer can read the code or ask their agent while answering. A wrong answer produces an explanation plus a new scenario on the same concept, and disputes and errors never count as passing. Five outcomes exist: correct answer, wrong answer, dispute question, pause check, and skip this time, where skips never count as passing. A pass lasts 24 hours unless the code, destination or policy changes; a matching push waits up to 25 minutes, and an agent shell may time out sooner. Question count scales with change size (small changes up to one question, documentation or trivial edits none, large changes up to three at default depth), and a separate distance setting (high for design, low for implementation detail, mixed by default) controls how close questions get to the code. Model review runs on the developer's own Claude Code or Codex plan allowance, on OpenRouter, or on any OpenAI-compatible endpoint; Sphinx has no account or hosted service of its own. A typical check makes about 5 to 8 requests plus roughly one per answer, and there is no default cap on model calls, so 'sphinx config --max-model-calls 30' (range 1 to 100) is available. Supported agents are Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and Pi, or plain Git without an agent. Per-repository files created by 'sphinx init' are .sphinxconfig (policy), .sphinxignore (paths never read) and .sphinxcontext.md (short project description sent with every reviewer request), and machine-wide settings live in ~/.config/sphinx/config.json. Privacy model: the reviewer provider receives the changed code and related files from the commit, the developer's answers and .sphinxcontext.md; ignored files are never read, and .env files, private keys and common credential files are excluded by default, but ignore rules match paths so a secret pasted into ordinary source still ships. Requirements are Node.js 22.19 or newer, Git, and macOS, Linux or WSL, with native Windows not supported yet. Version 0.1 covers local commits and pushes only, not web merges, CI-required checks or deployments, and cannot read binary file contents; with gh signed in a pass stamps the pushed commit and 'sphinx init --github-check' adds a Sphinx check to pull requests, but nothing ever blocks a push. The README states plainly that this is practice, not a security gate, since anyone with local access including a coding agent can bypass hooks, and that the examiner is an LLM and can be wrong. Source repository github.com/parthh01/sphinx (README read on 2026-10-23); project page https://sphinx-six-theta.vercel.app; npm package sphinx-understand, MIT licensed. Counterarguments raised on the HN thread and reflected in the post: the quiz tests the person rather than the diff, so a leftover debug print or a weakened assertion still ships; the questions are open book so a developer can ask their own agent for the answer; and a local hook is not enforceable against an agent that removes it. Lazy design: directory listings are read from Proton's metadata API and file bytes are downloaded on demand when a program opens a file, so there is no background full-drive sync job; writes are buffered to a local temp file and uploaded whole once the file closes after an upload delay. Remote changes arrive through Proton's event feed poll, which invalidates affected directory listings and cached file content. Architecture: applications talk to the kernel FUSE layer, which forwards to a single daemon (fusefs, drive and auth modules) that is the only component speaking the Proton API; the tray and any future GUI talk to that daemon over a local unix socket with a status file fallback. Requirements: Linux with FUSE 3 and access to /dev/fuse, optional Secret Service provider (GNOME Keyring, KWallet) and optional zenity. Commands: login, mount, unmount, tray, status, autostart, autostart -headless, logout, config init, config show. Session handling: the Proton password is never stored; the session file lives at $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/proton-drive-fs/session.json with mode 0600 inside a 0700 directory and holds a key password derived from the account password, which is moved into the OS keyring when a Secret Service provider is present, and logout removes both. Config file $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/proton-drive-fs/config.toml is created on first run with every key commented out at its default, precedence is flag over file over built-in default, and config show prints the merged values with their source. Key defaults verified from the usage page: ttl 30s, poll 10s, op-timeout 60s, cache-dir $XDG_CACHE_HOME/proton-drive-fs, cache-size 2GiB, large-file 300MiB, thumbnails true, upload-delay 5s, max-uploads 5, max-downloads 20, foreground false, log-level info. VERIFIED ON 2026-10-30: ULDA is Universal Linear Data Authentication, a three-part toolkit. ULDA Auth (npm ulda-auth 1.1.0, MIT-style API but see license below) is the client SDK for encrypted JSON resources over Socket.IO; ULDA Core (npm ulda-core 1.0.1) is the low-level protocol engine implementing the ULDA v1 state-lineage protocol; ULDA Server (v1.0.0, Docker Hub uldaio/ulda-server:1.0.0, TypeScript) stores opaque resources in PostgreSQL and notifies subscribers. ENCRYPTION VERIFIED: application content is encrypted client-side with AES-256-GCM; the server stores only ID, witness and opaque payload and cannot distinguish a master file from a content file. PROTOCOL VERIFIED from the MANIFEST: the default implementation profile is SHA-256 with N=5 and 256-bit origin blocks and the compactV1 codec; SHA-1 (code 0x01) is Web Crypto compatibility only and the manifest says it SHOULD NOT be used for new deployments. Two chain modes are documented: mode X permits one pending write per resource (adjacent-only) and mode S allows the next age at most 4 steps ahead of the confirmed age (skippable). A witness is derived from a private origin of five random blocks given different depths; the server hashes the four overlapping blocks once and compares, which is what stops a hostile server substituting an older or edited version. RUNTIME REQUIREMENTS VERIFIED: Node.js 22 or later, or a browser with ES2022, Web Crypto and WebSocket; ES modules with TypeScript declarations included. DEPLOYMENT VERIFIED: the published image contains only the application, the PostgreSQL adapter and the migration tools, NOT a database or reverse proxy; operators must supply their own PostgreSQL and an HTTPS/WSS endpoint, exactly one server writer against a database, and separate runtime and migration credentials. Local dev flow is docker compose build, up -d postgres, run --rm -e ULDA_DB_SETUP=1 db-setup, up -d --no-build, then GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/ready, where readiness includes a storage check. Browser clients need CORS_ORIGINS set to the exact origin including the port, and local HTTP requires the explicit allowInsecureLocalhost constructor option. The SDK is a client-side library and not a server runtime dependency. LICENSE RECORDED HONESTLY: all three repos (ulda-auth, ulda-core, ulda-server) carry a LICENSE.md identified as NOASSERTION by the GitHub license API, namely the ULDA Library Community Source License 1.0 version 1.0 dated 6 October 2026, which states in section 1 that it is a source-available license and NOT an OSI-approved open-source license. Commercial use is permitted for a Qualifying Small Organization, defined in section 4 by a Revenue Threshold of USD 1,000,000 consolidated gross revenue; crossing the threshold gives 90 calendar days to obtain a commercial license or stop exercising rights, and the license explicitly prohibits dividing or transferring revenue to avoid the threshold. Servers, container images, SaaS or API services and enterprise products require their own separate terms. The authors are Mark Shaposhnik (ULDA protocol and library concept) and Vitalii Radko (library implementation). SECURITY CAVEATS RECORDED IN THE POST from docs.ulda.io/sdk/security: on first open the client has no independently persisted witness or resource token so it trusts the server to return the requested master and substitution with another valid master under the same password is not fully prevented; there is no durable age anchor across closing the SDK or restarting the application so an old valid snapshot may be indistinguishable from the latest; Changed.deleted is a trusted server statement and not a cryptographic tombstone; a malicious server can withhold, corrupt or delete records, hide a newer valid version and deny service; the SDK implements no per-user roles, key revocation, password rotation or recovery of forgotten master credentials; there is no persistent offline write queue because the server rejects conflicting updates and the application handles resolution; client-side secrecy does not survive XSS, a malicious dependency, debugging access or a compromised OS since plaintext and origin bytes must be readable by JavaScript; a lost or malformed success ACK yields UNKNOWN_OUTCOME which is not proof of rollback and must not be retried automatically; and Changed is not a durable message log so a slow recipient can be disconnected. The SDK default timeout is 10 seconds per awaited transport operation, configurable from 50 to 60,000 ms, and automatic reconnect defaults to at most five attempts within 30 seconds; it rereads and verifies state and does not replay writes. Version compatibility caveat recorded: SDK 1.0.1 and earlier enforce the old small-catalog bound and cannot open catalogs that exceed it, so the server and all clients must be upgraded before catalogs grow past the old limits, and upgrading the SDK alone is insufficient for the large-operation transfer extension. VERIFIED ON 2026-10-30 from https://usefeyn.com/blog/feynobg/ (published July 21, 2026 by Hafedh Hichri and Shreyash Nigam of Feyn Labs). FeyNoBg is an open-source background removal model built on BiRefNet (Zheng et al., arXiv:2401.03407). BiRefNet splits the work between a localization module that finds the foreground and a reconstruction module that traces its boundary, both consuming feature maps from a four-stage Swin extractor. Feyn deepened the third stage from 18 to 24 blocks and injected six fresh blocks on top of the pretrained weights, taking the base configuration depths=[2, 2, 18, 2] to 263M parameters from 222M. The stated insight is that foreground recognition and boundary precision are taught with different focused data, so a narrow training mix produces unbalanced models; widening the mix turned an early DIS5K regression into one of four benchmark wins. PUBLISHED BENCHMARKS (S-measure, FeyNoBg vs the strongest published competitor): UHRSD-TE 0.981 vs BiRefNet 0.957, HRSOD-TE 0.983 vs S3ODNet 0.961, DIS5K 0.961 vs FlowDIS 0.951, DAVIS-S 0.977 vs BiRefNet 0.975, DUTS-TE 0.941 vs S3ODNet 0.949, COD10K-TE 0.912 vs S3ODNet 0.923, DUT-OMRON 0.883 vs S3ODNet 0.898, CAMO-TE 0.887 vs BiRefNet 0.904.
